children.description: UI content-related principles are associated with bugs that display abnormal UI elements.

Principles about abnormal textual contents shown on the UI, such as displaying raw error messages, complete blankness without warnings or meaningful messages, and text-quality issues including incomplete translation, truncated text, or garbled characters.

Principles about the visual style of UI elements, focusing on whether UI contents remain visible and recognizable (e.g., sufficient contrast) and whether a configurable theme is consistently applied to all UI components.

Principles about missing or duplicated UI elements that lead to abnormal UI displays, such as showing a blank screen (the whole screen completely empty) or showing more than one identical element on the UI, which can confuse users and hinder further interaction.

Principles about information consistency on the UI, where displayed information should not contradict the specified or expected criteria (e.g., sorting of list items matches the sorting criteria) and should remain coherent with user-visible settings (e.g., consistent language display).

Principles about abnormal media-related UI content, where images, videos, icons, or previews are displayed in an unexpected way (e.g., distorted scaling or missing/blank previews), resulting in misleading or unusable UI elements.

Interaction-related principles involve the semantics of user interactions rather than UI display. Interaction-related principles are applied to a series of actions within applications rather than a single state.

Principles related to screen rotation operations, where users generally expect rotation to only affect UI layout but not UI contents; because Android may destroy and recreate the current activity, incorrect data persistence may lead to changes in UI states, such as user inputs, floating dialogs, or even different pages.

Principles about basic interaction usability, where users expect apps to respond to operations via actionable UI elements and not get stuck in infinite loading, since such behaviors prevent users from properly completing the intended functionality.

Principles about navigation semantics, where users share a clear and accurate expectation of navigation behavior (e.g., the back button should take the user to the logically previous screen and close the most recent dialogs/menus first), and interacting with highlighted links should navigate to the corresponding webpage.

Principles about setting-related interaction semantics, where users expect that once they have modified settings, the application will remember and apply them consistently across sessions, and that changing language settings will switch the UI accordingly.

Principles about CRUD-like interaction operations, where users expect actions such as save/delete to take effect correctly and the resulting state to remain consistent (e.g., deleted items should not reappear unless intentionally restored).

Principles about preserving UI state and user data across interaction sequences and lifecycle events, where incorrect data persistence may lead to changes in UI states such as user inputs, floating dialogs, or different pages.

Principles about text-entry interaction semantics, where users expect stable input/editing behavior (e.g., cursor/edit actions behave as intended) and that inputs are not unexpectedly lost or altered during interaction flows.

Principles about data-transfer interaction workflows (import/export/download/upload), where users expect these operations to complete correctly and, when failures occur (e.g., external exceptions), the app should not leave users without meaningful feedback.

Principles about interactions that depend on system-level features (e.g., notifications and keyboard behavior), where understanding interactive semantics across app–OS boundaries is required to judge whether the behavior is erroneous.

Principles about keeping UI states consistent during a series of actions, where the UI indicators (e.g., component/button/notification states) should remain aligned with the actual app state rather than drifting across interaction sequences.

Principles about touch/gesture interaction semantics via actionable UI elements, where users expect the app to respond appropriately to touches (e.g., clicks, long-press, scrolling) rather than leaving the screen unchanged or triggering misaligned effects.

Principles about media-playback interaction semantics, where users expect playback controls and playback state (e.g., position and progress) to behave smoothly and predictably during interaction sequences.
Principles about other common interaction purposes that are widely used in apps but are not covered by the listed subcategories, grouped as a catch-all for frequent everyday functions.

Principles about permission, security, and account-management interaction semantics, where users expect permission prompts and authentication/account flows to behave coherently and reliably across interaction sequences.

Principles about file-handling interaction operations (e.g., renaming, selecting, sharing, saving), where users expect safe and correct behavior such as avoiding unintended overwrites and preserving file identity and content.
UI layout-related principles are associated with bugs that cause UI elements to be rendered at incorrect positions or for content to overflow beyond element boundaries.
Principles about abnormal UI layout related to element sizes, where texts should be displayed clearly and integrally and should not be cropped.

Principles about abnormal UI layout related to positions and overlapping, where visible views should not overlap and visible UI components should not be obscured, since overlapping/obscuring can make contents incomplete or hard to read.

Principles about adapting layout when content overflows or the UI must reflow (e.g., after screen rotation), where the app should redraw UI elements by resizing or repositioning them; otherwise obvious display issues may occur (e.g., elements shifting out of view) or text wrapping may become extremely unreadable (e.g., splitting words in the middle).
